## Appendix A Limitations

Our study has several limitations. First, due to computing-resource constraints, the Code-X training recipe is only validated at the 9B and 27B scales (Qwen-3.5-9B and Qwen-3.6-27B), and we have not yet characterized how the recipe scales to frontier-size open-source models. Second, due to API credit constraints, several closed-source coding agents could not be evaluated on the full benchmark suite. In particular, Claude Opus 4.6 results on VideoZeroBench and Claude Opus 4.7 results across all four benchmarks are incomplete in the current draft, which means the comparison between coding agents and native omni-modal models is somewhat uneven on the closed-source side. Third, our scope is restricted to offline omni-modal tasks, where files are staged into a workspace ahead of time; conclusions do not transfer directly to streaming or interactive settings.

## Appendix B Broader Impacts

Our findings establish a more compute- and token-efficient pathway for offline omni-modal understanding, showing that text+image coding agents with sandboxed tool use can match or surpass native omni-modal models on many video- and audio-centric tasks while consuming fewer tokens. This lowers the resource barrier for omni-modal applications and broadens access for researchers and users who lack dedicated omni-model APIs, while our open-sourced Code-X recipe, OmniCoding dataset, and TerminalBench-O benchmark further support reproducible research at the model–tool–environment interface. As with any tool-using agent that processes video and audio, downstream deployments should incorporate standard safeguards such as content provenance, access controls, and user consent; we note that our agents operate only on user-staged files within an isolated workspace and do not autonomously take real-world actions.

## Appendix C Adapting Sandboxed Agents for Omni-Modal Tasks

We represent each omni-modal task as

 x=(q,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{Y}), 

where q is a natural-language instruction, \mathcal{F} is a set of input files, and
 \mathcal{Y} is the set of acceptable final answers. We use an answer set rather than a
single reference string so that aliases, option letters, numerical formats, and unit variants can
be handled uniformly in both evaluation and reinforcement learning.

A native omni-modal model solves the task by packing the files into model context:

 \hat{y}_{\mathrm{omni}}=M_{\theta}\!\left(\mathrm{Pack}(q,\mathcal{F})\right), 

where \mathrm{Pack}(\cdot) denotes model-specific media encoding, sampling, and serialization.
In this formulation, video and audio are first-class model inputs.

In contrast, our sandboxed agent does not need to ingest all raw media as context. The files
 \mathcal{F} are staged into an isolated workspace, and the agent is given the instruction and
the corresponding file paths. It then interacts with the workspace through a terminal interface:
it can inspect files, invoke tools such as ffmpeg, ffprobe, OCR, or ASR systems,
write and execute scripts, create intermediate artifacts, and finally submit an answer.

A sandbox rollout is written as

 \tau=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T}), 

where o_{t} is the current observation, including command outputs and workspace feedback, and
 a_{t} is the agent’s next message or terminal action. During a rollout, raw omni-modal files may
be converted into task-relevant artifacts such as transcripts, sampled frames, OCR text, timestamps,
